title: Change Counter
context: Grade 4, the taking-away half of the chapter's middle section. An adult sees change being counted out. What is actually being settled is where paise come from when there are too few on top: one rupee is broken into a hundred paise, and the rupees go down by one. The chapter works that once, with paise on both lines. The exercise then asks for change from whole-rupee payments, which takes paise from zero paise, and the one worked example that does so prints only its answer. It is the same move, a rupee broken into a hundred paise, and this tool works it in full every time. The exercise asks for the amount returned, so the total of the bill is a step and not the answer.

writeup.why: Take one amount from another in columns, break a rupee into a hundred paise whenever the paise on top are too few, and find the change a payment brings back.
writeup.look: A shop counter with the money given on the left, the bill beside it, a column frame between them, and a change tray at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Change Counter' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the columns taken away against the two columns in the frame, paise and rupees, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each column's answer lands and the second fixed at two. On the fourth phase the check is counted as a third step, so the second number reads three. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The money given lies at the left of the working area, 260 by 240 at 64,214, as the notes paid laid side by side with their amount written under them in deep blue. The bill slip lies under it, 260 by 260 at 64,466, listing the things and their prices with the total at its foot. The column frame stands in the middle, 480 by 500 at 344,214: the money given on the top line and the bill on the second, a near-black dotted line down the frame so that every dot sits on it, rupees to its left and paise to its right, a rule under the second line and the answer line under the rule. A whole-rupee amount stands in the frame with grey zeros filling its paise column. The take-away control sits at the foot of the frame, 220 by 56 at 344,658, and works the paise column first. When the paise on top are fewer than the paise below, the paise cell stays shut and the break control lights over the rupees on top, 220 by 56 at 604,658. Break strikes through the rupees figure on top and writes the figure one less above it in amber; one rupee rises from the struck figure and opens into a strip of a hundred cells that slides across the dotted line to join the paise on top, whose figure is rewritten a hundred more above them in amber. From zero paise the strip alone becomes the paise on top, a hundred paise. Only then does the paise cell open, and after it the rupees. The change tray stands at the right, 300 by 340 at 850,214, and fills with the change, the rupees as play notes and coins and the paise as shaded cells on one strip, with the change written under it in reddish purple. The check control sits under the tray, 300 by 60 at 850,570, slides the change back across onto the bill, adds the two in columns, and lays the sum beside the money given. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across with a dot key, and the answer slot prints Rs before the number and holds exactly two places after the dot. On the fourth phase the slot's label reads change, so the bill's total, which the frame shows as a step, has a place of its own that is not the answer. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue. The paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion, a clear round dot, and wherever amounts stand in columns it sits on a near-black dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count of things is not money. The zeros that fill the paise column of a whole-rupee amount in column working are grey. Every play note is one plain pale blue rectangle and every play coin one plain steel disc, all notes one size and all coins one size, each printed with its value and nothing else. No coin below one rupee is drawn anywhere: paise are shaded cells on a strip ruled into a hundred in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every column rule, dotted line, tick, bracket, strike line, bill rule and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in, a count by the box beside the times sign or the slot marked things, and the change or money left by the tray or line that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in a paise column is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. The rupees figure on top is never rubbed out: it is struck through once and the figure one less written above it, so a break can be read after the take-away is done. A strip of a hundred cells crosses the dotted line only when a rupee is broken, and the paise cell opens only when the paise on top are at least the paise below.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last take-away the child worked, every broken rupee struck through and rewritten, the change in the tray, and the check adding back to the money given.

phases.win: the paise answer lands, then the rupees answer beside it across the dot
phases.does: takes away the paise column, then the rupees column
phases.goal: amounts are taken away in columns with the dots in a line, the paise first and then the rupees
phases.says: Which column do you take away first?
phases.check: Away from the screen: take Rs 12.30 from Rs 47.85, paise first.
phases.feels: each column takes away on its own, and the paise go first
phases.hands: Play shopkeeper with play notes, coins and paper strips of a hundred cells. Price a toy at Rs 23.40 and lay Rs 48.65 of play money on the counter, then take the price away in columns on the board, paise first and then rupees. Count out what is left from the play money to check the board.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which amount is on top? Second rung, the phase's: which column did you take away first? Third rung: the frame is cut to an amount whose bottom line has no rupees, only paise, and the child takes the paise away before the full amounts come back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the rupees are the big part of each amount, and the paise look like a small tail that can be dropped.
wrong.move: takes away the rupees only and writes Rs 45, leaving the paise out.
wrong.screen: the paise column lights green and its take-away runs, forty less fifteen, and twenty-five lands on the answer line after the dot. The answer line then reads rupees, dot and paise, and the child's Rs 45 stays in the slot beside it, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the first amount heard is the first one written, and the word from is easy to pass over.
wrong.move: sets Rs 23.15 on the top line because it was named first in take Rs 23.15 from Rs 68.40.
wrong.screen: the frame sets the child's order and the take-away tries the rupees: twenty-three rupees on top cannot give sixty-eight, and the rupees cell stays shut. The word from in the question lights, the two lines change places so that the amount after it stands on top, and the child's first frame stays drawn beside the new one.

phases.screen: the column frame holding a larger amount above a smaller one, with enough paise on top
phases.soWhat: Take away the paise first, then the rupees, with the dots in one line.

phases.win: the rupee opens into a hundred cells, the paise on top grow by a hundred, and the take-away goes through
phases.does: breaks one rupee, watches the rupees go down by one and the paise on top grow by a hundred, then takes away
phases.goal: when the paise on top are too few, one rupee is broken into a hundred paise and the rupees on top go down by one
phases.says: There are not enough paise on top. Where can more come from?
phases.check: Take Rs 19.75 from Rs 53.40. Say where the extra paise came from.
phases.feels: the rupee does not vanish, it moves across the dot as a hundred paise
phases.hands: Give a pair Rs 5.20 in play money, five rupee coins and a strip with twenty cells shaded, and ask them to pay seventy paise. They cannot from twenty cells, so they swap one rupee coin for a full strip of a hundred cells. Count the paise now, a hundred and twenty, and take seventy away. Ask how many rupee coins are left.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: are there enough paise on top? Second rung, the phase's: what does one rupee become? Third rung: the frame is cut to one rupee and twenty paise on top and fifty paise below, and the child breaks the rupee before the larger take-away comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the paise column holds two numbers, and taking the smaller from the larger is the only take-away that seems to work, whichever line each is on.
wrong.move: takes the smaller paise from the larger, eighty-five less thirty, whichever line each stands on, and writes Rs 288.55.
wrong.screen: the paise cell stays shut on the thirty on top, and the child's fifty-five is written small beside it. The break control then strikes through four hundred and twenty-six and writes four hundred and twenty-five above it, and a strip of a hundred cells joins the thirty to make a hundred and thirty. The paise take away, a hundred and thirty less eighty-five, and the child's Rs 288.55 stays in the slot.

wrong.why: breaking a rupee is heard as making a hundred paise, and the thirty already there is easy to lose as the new figure is written.
wrong.move: breaks the rupee but writes a hundred paise in place of the thirty on top, instead of adding them, and gets Rs 287.15.
wrong.screen: the strip of a hundred cells slides across and lies beside the thirty shaded cells on top, and the two are counted together, a hundred and thirty, before anything is taken. The paise take away, a hundred and thirty less eighty-five, and the child's Rs 287.15 stays in the slot beside the new answer.

phases.screen: a take-away whose paise on top are fewer than the paise below, with the paise cell refusing
phases.soWhat: When the paise on top are fewer than the paise below, break one rupee into a hundred paise. The rupees on top go down by one.

phases.win: a hundred paise appear on top, the rupees go down by one, and both columns take away
phases.does: breaks one rupee, sees a hundred paise appear on top, takes the paise away, then the rupees
phases.goal: from zero paise, one rupee is broken into a hundred paise, so the rupees go down by one and the paise on top become a hundred
phases.says: The top has no paise at all. What do you break?
phases.check: Take Rs 36.20 from Rs 100. What is written above the rupees, and what above the paise?
phases.feels: with no paise on top, the break makes all of them, and the rupees pay for it
phases.hands: Write Rs 200 on the board with two zeros in its paise column, 200.00, and ask the class to take forty-five paise away. Let them find that there are zero paise on top. Then break one rupee: strike through the two hundred, write one hundred and ninety-nine above it, and write a hundred paise above the zeros. Take forty-five from the hundred.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many paise are on top? Second rung, the phase's: where can paise come from when there are none? Third rung: the frame is cut to one rupee, written with two zeros in its paise column, with ten paise below, and the child breaks it before the larger take-away comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: with nothing on top in the paise column, the paise below look as if there is nothing to take them from, so they come down as they are.
wrong.move: writes the thirty-five paise from the bottom line straight down into the answer, and gets Rs 243.35.
wrong.screen: the paise cell stays shut over the grey zeros, and the child's thirty-five is written small beside it. The break control then strikes through three hundred and writes two hundred and ninety-nine above it, and a full strip of a hundred cells slides across to stand over the zeros, a hundred paise on top. A hundred less thirty-five is taken away, and the child's Rs 243.35 stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the hundred paise are the part that gets written, and the rupee they came from is easy to forget to take off.
wrong.move: breaks a rupee into a hundred paise but leaves the three hundred as it was, and gets Rs 243.65.
wrong.screen: the three hundred on top is lit with nothing struck through it, beside a hundred paise that came from nowhere, and the whole top line is counted in paise to show it has grown by a rupee. The three hundred is then struck through and two hundred and ninety-nine written above it, and the take-away runs again, the child's Rs 243.65 staying in the slot.

phases.screen: a whole-rupee amount written with two zeros in its paise column, above an amount with paise
phases.soWhat: To take paise from zero paise, break one rupee into a hundred paise. The rupees go down by one, and the paise on top become a hundred.

phases.win: the change fills the tray, and the change and the bill add back to the money given
phases.does: sets the bill under the money given, takes it away, counts the change into the tray, then adds it back to check
phases.goal: the change is the money given less the bill, and adding the change back to the bill checks it
phases.says: What was paid, and what was the bill? How much comes back?
phases.check: A bill comes to Rs 184.75 and a Rs 200 note is paid. What is the change? Add it back to check.
phases.feels: the change is what the money given still holds once the bill has been paid out of it
phases.hands: Price three things on a play counter so that the bill comes to rupees and paise, and pay with large play notes. The shopkeeper adds the bill, takes it from the money given in columns, and counts the change out. The shopper then adds the change to the bill aloud and checks that it makes the money given.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what was paid, and what was the bill? Second rung, the phase's: which is taken from which? Third rung: the counter is cut to a bill in whole rupees paid with one note, and the child finds the change and adds it back before the larger bill comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: adding the bill was the long part of the work and its total is the last big number written, so it feels like the end.
wrong.move: gives the bill, Rs 736.40, as the answer, when the question asks how much change comes back.
wrong.screen: the child's number is set against the bill slip's total, where it matches, and the answer slot's label, change, lights in reddish purple. The bill is then set under the money given, eight hundred rupees, and taken away, and the change tray fills. The child's Rs 736.40 stays in the slot beside the bill's own total.

wrong.why: a bill and a payment are both money on the counter, and adding is what was just done to the bill.
wrong.move: adds the bill to the money given and writes Rs 1536.40.
wrong.screen: the check control lays the child's sum beside the notes paid, and it stands far taller than the eight hundred rupees on the counter, more than the shopper ever had. The bill is then set under the money given and taken away, a rupee broken into a hundred paise at the paise column, and the change fills the tray. The child's number stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a bill slip with its total, the notes paid, and the change tray empty
phases.soWhat: The change is the money given less the bill, and adding the change back to the bill checks it.

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, the moment the check control is pressed on a bill with paise that was paid in whole rupees. The change slides back across the counter onto the bill, and its shaded cells pour onto the bill's paise and fill exactly one strip, not a cell over and not a cell short. The full strip curls up into a rupee and joins the rupees, and the whole stack settles level beside the notes that were paid, rupee for rupee. It can be run as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the column frame holds a larger amount above a smaller one, with enough paise on top, and the take-away control lit. On the second the frame holds a take-away whose paise on top are fewer than the paise below, the paise cell shut and the break control waiting over the rupees on top. On the third the top line is a whole-rupee amount carrying two zeros in its paise column, as column working writes it, above an amount with paise. On the fourth a bill slip lies under the notes paid, the frame is empty and the change tray stands empty at the right. The running count at the top left holds the columns taken away against the columns in the frame, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the paise column, or the break control, or the grey zeros, or the bill slip, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which column goes first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any payment and any bill, with the break control, the change tray and the check open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on taking away paise first, breaking a rupee into a hundred paise, taking paise from zero paise by the same break, and finding and checking change.
voiceLines: Money given, a bill, and a tray for the change. Which column goes first?
Which column do you take away first?
There are not enough paise on top. Where can more come from?
The top has no paise at all. What do you break?
What was paid, and what was the bill? How much comes back?
A new bill. Set it under the money given before anything is taken.
Free play. Any payment and any bill, with the break, the tray and the check open.
Look at the paise on top again. Are there enough to take from?
A rupee broken wherever the paise were too few, and every change added back to check.

observations.why: Each column is taken away on its own, and the paise go first because a break, when one is needed, starts there.
observations.soWhat: Take away the paise first, then the rupees, with the dots in one line.
observations.observe: The paise answer landed first, then the rupees answer beside it across the dot.

observations.why: The broken rupee became a hundred paise that joined the paise on top, so it left the rupees.
observations.soWhat: When the paise on top are fewer than the paise below, break one rupee into a hundred paise. The rupees on top go down by one.
observations.observe: The paise cell stayed shut until a rupee was broken, and then the rupees on top showed one less.

observations.why: There were no paise on top for the strip to join, so its hundred cells were all there was.
observations.soWhat: To take paise from zero paise, break one rupee into a hundred paise. The rupees go down by one, and the paise on top become a hundred.
observations.observe: From zero paise, the strip from the broken rupee alone made the paise on top, a hundred paise.

observations.why: The change is what the money given still holds once the bill is taken out, so putting the bill back gives it all again.
observations.soWhat: The change is the money given less the bill, and adding the change back to the bill checks it.
observations.observe: The change slid back onto the bill, and the two made exactly the money given.

source_tool.description: A shop counter fills the stage. The money given lies on the left as notes, the bill slip lies beside it, and a column frame between them sets the bill under the money given with the dots in one line. The take-away control works the paise column first. When the paise on top are fewer than the paise below, the paise cell will not take away. A break control then lifts one rupee from the rupees on top: the old rupees figure is struck through and the figure one less written above it, as the chapter's own regrouping example sets them, and the rupee opens into a strip of a hundred cells that joins the paise on top. From zero paise, the broken rupee alone becomes the paise on top, a hundred paise. Only then does the paise column take away, and after it the rupees column. A change tray at the right fills with the change, the rupees as notes and coins and the paise as shaded cells on a strip, and a check control adds the change back to the bill and lays the sum beside the money given.
source_tool.art_direction: A shop counter with a change tray / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a rupee tray and a paise tray, strips ruled into a hundred cells, a counting tray of value slots, a bill slip with a dotted line, a shop counter with a change tray, a multiplying frame under a row of things, and a till with a share mat.

Every note and coin shows its value in large figures and nothing else: no design, no picture, no lettering but the value. Every note is a plain paper rectangle and every coin a plain metal disc, all notes one size and one colour and all coins one size and one metal, so a value is read from its print and never from size or colour.

No coin below one rupee is drawn or named anywhere. Wherever paise are drawn rather than written, they are shaded cells on a rupee strip ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Nothing standing for paise is ever round.

Written money with paise is Rs, the rupees, a dot and two digits of paise, as Rs 96.75. Fewer than ten paise are written with a zero in the first place after the dot. A whole amount in running text is written with no dot, as Rs 43.

Column working always stands on a dotted line: every dot in a column sits on it, rupees to its left and paise to its right. In column working a whole-rupee amount carries two zeros in its paise column, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit.

A hundred paise rolling up into one rupee is always shown moving, from the paise column into a small carry circle over the rupees, and a rupee broken into paise is always shown opening into a full strip of a hundred cells.
A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through and the new figure written above it, never erased, so the break can be read afterwards.
The number of things in a product is a count. It stands in a box of its own beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns, with no dot, and no cell exists for it under the paise.
Every answer slot carries its unit, rupees or things, printed beside the number.
A total, a change, a cost or an amount left is told apart by the slot or line it sits in first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a note, a coin, a cell or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue, and the paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion in every tool, drawn as a clear round dot on the dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count is never money. The two zeros in the paise column of a whole-rupee amount are grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded. Every play note is one plain pale blue and every play coin one plain steel, so a value is read from its print and never from its colour. All of that holds in greyscale, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in and a count by the box beside the times sign, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the paise on top again. Are there enough to take from?
voice.onNext: A new bill. Set it under the money given before anything is taken.
voice.opening: Money given, a bill, and a tray for the change. Which column goes first?
voice.onFinish: A rupee broken wherever the paise were too few, and every change added back to check.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any payment and any bill, with the break, the tray and the check open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

placement.where: After a shopkeeper and a shopper have made change with play money for a price in rupees and paise, and the shopper has broken a rupee into a hundred-cell strip by hand. The tool is what refuses to take paise from too few paise until a rupee is broken, which working on paper lets a child skip.

answer_key.rule: To take one amount from another, write the smaller under the larger with the dots in one line, and take away the paise first, then the rupees. When the paise on top are fewer than the paise below, break one rupee into a hundred paise: the rupees on top go down by one and the paise on top grow by a hundred. From zero paise the same move gives a hundred paise on top, so Rs 500, written 500.00 in column working, becomes Rs 499 and 100 paise. The change is the money given less the bill. Adding the change back to the bill gives the money given, which checks it.
answer_key.wrong: The rupee is broken again at walking pace, the rupees on top going down by one and a strip of a hundred cells joining the paise on top, and the two columns are taken away again in turn. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Write Rs 23.15 under Rs 68.40 with the dots in one line.
Then rupees: 68 less 23 is 45. The answer is Rs 45.25.
items.question: Take Rs 23.15 from Rs 68.40.
items.checkpoint: Take away the paise first, then the rupees.
items.misconception: Taking away the rupees only and writing Rs 45, leaving the paise out.

steps: Paise first: 85 paise cannot be taken from 30 paise.
Break one rupee into a hundred paise: Rs 426 and 30 paise become Rs 425 and 130 paise.
130 less 85 is 45 paise, and 425 less 138 is 287 rupees. The answer is Rs 287.45.
items.question: Take Rs 138.85 from Rs 426.30.
items.checkpoint: When the paise on top are too few, break one rupee into a hundred paise; the rupees on top go down by one.
items.misconception: Taking the smaller paise from the larger, 85 less 30, and writing Rs 288.55.

steps: In column working, Rs 300 is written 300.00, with two zeros in the paise column.
There are zero paise on top, so break one rupee into a hundred paise: Rs 299 and 100 paise.
100 less 35 is 65 paise, and 299 less 57 is 242 rupees. The answer is Rs 242.65.
items.question: Take Rs 57.35 from Rs 300.
items.checkpoint: From zero paise, break one rupee into a hundred paise; the rupees go down by one.
items.misconception: Writing the 35 paise from the bottom, which gives Rs 243.35, or breaking the rupee and not taking it off the rupees, which gives Rs 243.65.

steps: The money given is Rs 500 and Rs 300, which is Rs 800. The change is the money given less the bill.
Rs 800 is written 800.00. From zero paise, break one rupee into a hundred paise: Rs 799 and 100 paise.
100 less 40 is 60 paise, and 799 less 736 is 63. The change is Rs 63.60. Check: Rs 63.60 and Rs 736.40 make Rs 800.
items.question: A bill comes to Rs 736.40. The shopper pays with one Rs 500 note and three Rs 100 notes. How much change comes back?
items.checkpoint: The change is the money given less the bill; adding the change back to the bill gives the money given.
items.misconception: Giving the bill, Rs 736.40, as the answer, or adding the bill to the money given.

items.question: Take Rs 27.80 from Rs 64.25.

items.question: Take Rs 315.95 from Rs 540.60.

items.question: A child takes Rs 125.30 from Rs 600 and writes Rs 475.30. What went wrong, and what is the right answer?
items.final_answer: The child wrote the 30 paise from the bottom instead of taking them away. From zero paise, break one rupee into a hundred paise: Rs 599 and 100 paise. 100 less 30 is 70 and 599 less 125 is 474, so the answer is Rs 474.70

items.question: A bag costs Rs 348.50, shoes Rs 525.25 and socks Rs 64.60. The shopper pays Rs 1200 for all three. How much is returned?
items.final_answer: Rs 261.65. The bill comes to Rs 938.35, and Rs 1200 less Rs 938.35 is Rs 261.65. The bill is a step; the question asks for the amount returned

items.question: A shopper pays with a Rs 500 note for a bill of Rs 412.85 and is handed Rs 87.15. Is the change right? Check by adding.
items.final_answer: Yes. Rs 87.15 and Rs 412.85 make Rs 500.00, which is the money given

teaching_notes: Play shopkeeper and shopper with play notes and hundred-cell strips before the tool is opened: a price in rupees and paise, a large note, and the change counted out. Then use the tool for the one move paper lets a child skip, breaking a rupee. The chapter's regrouping example breaks one rupee into a hundred paise when there are too few paise on top, and the rupees go down by one. That example has paise on both lines. Both bills in the exercise are paid in whole rupees and come to rupees and paise, so paise are taken from zero paise, and the chapter's only worked example of that prints the answer with no working. It is the same move: break one rupee into a hundred paise, the rupees go down by one, and the paise on top become a hundred. Work it in full on the board, more than once. The exercise asks for the amount returned; the bill's total is a step, and a child who stops there has answered a different question. Adding the change back to the bill checks every answer.
generation_prompt: Build a change-giving tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. The working area is a shop counter: the money given lies on the left as notes with its amount written under them, the bill slip lies beside it with its total, and a column frame between them sets the bill under the money given with the dots in one line, a whole-rupee amount carrying two zeros in its paise column. A take-away control works the paise column first. When the paise on top are fewer than the paise below, the paise cell will not take away, and a break control lifts one rupee from the rupees on top: the old rupees figure is struck through, the figure one less is written above it, and the rupee opens into a strip of a hundred cells that joins the paise on top, so from zero paise the break makes a hundred paise on top. Then the paise column and the rupees column take away in turn. A change tray at the right fills with the change, rupees as notes and coins and paise as shaded cells on a strip, and a check control adds the change back to the bill and lays the sum beside the money given. No coin below one rupee appears. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Line up the dots. Take away the paise first. If the paise on top are too few, break one rupee into a hundred paise. The change is the money given less the bill. Add it back to check.
